content: West Nile Virus (WNV) was first identified in 1937 when it was isolated from a hospitalized patient in the West Nile district of Uganda. The patient presented with an isolated fever. Between the 1950s and 1960s, repeated outbreaks occurred in small villages within the Mediterranean basin, particularly in Israel and Egypt. These outbreaks provided researchers with opportunities to study the molecular and clinical characteristics of the virus, its transmission mechanisms, and its natural history. During the latter half of the 20th century, additional outbreaks were documented in Europe, the Middle East, the Far East, and Africa. However, it was not until 1999 that the first outbreak in the United States was recorded, marking the virus's emergence as a global infection. The most severe outbreak occurred in the United States in 2002, which saw the highest number of cases of meningoencephalitis from a single WNV outbreak. That same year, the first documented cases of person-to-person transmission were reported, involving blood transfusions and tissue transplantation. The discovery of WNV dates back to its isolation in 1937 from a patient in Uganda who exhibited an isolated fever. Early descriptions of the virus noted similarities to St. Louis encephalitis virus and Japanese B encephalitis virus. Initial studies highlighted the virus's neurotropism, as central nervous system (CNS) involvement was frequently observed in infected patients. However, it was during the Mediterranean basin outbreaks of the 1950s and 1960s that the clinical and pathological features of WNV were more thoroughly characterized. The first documented epidemic occurred in Israel in 1951, where Bernkopf and colleagues isolated WNV from 123 cases. Subsequent studies during outbreaks in Cairo, Egypt, between 1951 and 1954 provided further insights into the virus's transmission patterns and pathogenesis. In 1957, during another outbreak in Israel, the first reports of neurological complications following WNV infection were documented. Additional outbreaks were reported in Europe, India, and South Africa during the 1970s and 1980s. A significant outbreak in Romania in 1996 triggered a series of outbreaks across the Middle East, North Africa, and Europe. Unlike earlier outbreaks, which primarily affected children, these later outbreaks revealed a predominance of adult cases and a higher incidence of CNS complications. In 1999, the first outbreak in the United States was reported in Queens, New York City, involving eight cases, most of which presented with neurological symptoms. This outbreak marked the global spread of WNV. A total of 62 individuals were eventually infected, with severe symptoms requiring hospitalization. Initially thought to be caused by an endemic arbovirus, WNV was identified as the causative agent after a concurrent outbreak among birds in the same region and time frame was discovered. By 2002, the most severe WNV outbreak occurred in North America, with the largest number of meningoencephalitis cases recorded from a single outbreak. That same year, human-to-human transmission via blood transfusion and tissue transplantation was first documented. The development of diagnostic and treatment strategies for WNV has been significant. The first commercial diagnostic test for arboviruses, based on MAC-ELISA, was developed and later adapted for field use. Following the 1999 outbreak in the United States, the first animal vaccine for WNV was created and subsequently approved by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). The WNV-DNA vaccine remains the only USDA-approved vaccine for the virus. The 1999 outbreak in New York had a profound impact on public health and cultural history. It prompted the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to establish a Zoo Surveillance Program at Cornell University’s School of Veterinary Medicine. During the outbreak, the CDC also utilized other channels to test infected bird species to aid in identifying the virus. Delays in diagnosis were considered a critical factor contributing to the outbreak's severity. Following this event, WNV was designated a nationally reportable disease in the United States. Annual meetings were held to disseminate public health information, and guidelines for surveillance, prevention, and control of WNV were developed and regularly updated. In 2000, the CDC launched ArboNET, a real-time disease reporting network designed to monitor WNV infections in humans and animals. Funding for the CDC’s Enhanced Laboratory Capacity (ELC) cooperative agreement program reached $2.7 million in 2000 and exceeded $20 million in subsequent years. These funds were used to train arbovirologists, support research initiatives, and enhance laboratory diagnostics and surveillance programs.
